title: Rearchitecting a Neuromorphic Processor for Spike-Driven Brain-Computer Interfacing
problem: Processor design for spike-driven brain-computer interface signal processing remains unexplored; as BCIs scale to larger electrode arrays, spike-driven processing becomes attractive but requires specialized hardware architecture.
motivation: Scaled BCIs with more electrodes need efficient processing where computations are offloaded to a processor upon spike detection rather than processing continuously.
method: NeuroLobe redesigns a neuromorphic processor—specialized hardware that naturally processes spike signals from the brain—to efficiently handle brain-computer interface signal processing. It extends the processor's instruction set so programmers can deploy different algorithms flexibly. The design speeds up data movement between components, adds a synchronization unit to coordinate large numbers of spikes from electrode arrays, includes software for load balancing, and uses a multitask controller to run multiple algorithms simultaneously.
key_novelty: NeuroLobe adapts a neuromorphic processor's spike-handling ability for brain-computer interfaces, combining hardware and software design to enable flexible algorithm deployment.
contributions: ISA extension enabling flexible deployment of spike-driven BCI algorithms
Redesigned connection controller and execution path improving performance
Custom synchronization unit for scalable spike-driven processing
Software stack minimizing load imbalance across cores and multitask controller for parallel algorithms
limitations: Design tradeoffs and scalability limitations not discussed in abstract.
primary_theme: neuromorphic processor architecture for spike-driven BCI
